target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove scheduling barriers and give most voters uninterrupted time to vote
objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other service jobs would still be scheduled to work and would face a wages-versus-voting tradeoff. In other words, the holiday does not reliably eliminate the scheduling barrier; it can simply shift it into lost-pay pressure for workers least able to absorb it.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not meaningfully reduce the scheduling barrier unless employers are legally forced to shut down or give paid leave
objection: The argument assumes that a holiday only matters if it mandates employer shutdown or paid leave, but the real barrier is ordinary day-of attendance expectations. Declaring Election Day a holiday changes those expectations by making schools close and encouraging employers and co-workers to accommodate voting time, so the holiday can still meaningfully reduce the conflict even without a paid-leave mandate.

target: AG1’s assumption that a federal holiday reliably reduces required attendance for most voters
objection: A holiday is only a public designation; it does not require private employers to shut down or to provide paid time off. Because retail, restaurant, caregiving, and other essential/service workplaces often remain open, many workers would still be scheduled through polling hours, so the holiday would not reliably create the uninterrupted access AG1 assumes.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only works if it compels shutdowns or paid leave
objection: That view is too narrow because many voting barriers come from coordinating work, school, childcare, and household responsibilities on a normal weekday. A national holiday aligns those schedules for many families and caregivers, creating a practical window to vote even if employers are not legally required to pay everyone to do so.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday will not reliably reduce the day-of scheduling conflict because private employers can still schedule workers
objection: The rebuttal points out that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, which suggests that moving elections off a normal work/school day is a reliable and workable way to improve access even though private employers still exist and still schedule labor.

target: AG2’s claim that workers will still face a full-day attendance choice on a federal holiday
objection: This assumes a holiday does not change scheduling in practice, but federal holidays usually do create a day-of scheduling reset: schools close and many employers reduce hours or staffing. For many workers, that means the voting conflict is materially eased rather than simply shifted into an unpaid attendance dilemma.

target: AG1’s claim that Election Day should be a national holiday because it would directly increase turnout and solve scheduling barriers
objection: Research suggests that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to raise turnout compared with more targeted voting-access reforms. Since a calendar change alone does not address registration, alternative voting routes, or actual workplace accommodations, it is a low-impact and inefficient policy relative to options like employer time-off laws, early voting, vote-by-mail, or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is a low-impact reform and that it disadvantages low-income workers
objection: The holiday does directly address the day-of attendance problem: schools close, many workplaces alter schedules, and voters with limited ability to take time off get more practical access to the polls. Far from disadvantaging low-income workers, it can help them because they are often the least able to vote on a normal workday without special leave.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would reset the day’s obligations and not disadvantage low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to shut down or provide paid leave, so low-wage workers in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and similar jobs may still be scheduled and still lose pay if they vote. That means the supposed scheduling reset is not reliable, and the holiday can preserve or worsen the wage-versus-voting burden for those workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully changes the operating day for a large share of the public and is not merely symbolic
objection: Treating Election Day as a holiday does not necessarily pause the operating day for the people who most need flexibility, because many private employers continue normal operations and do not grant paid time to vote. The calendar changes, but the actual day-of constraint for many workers remains intact.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday removes major practical barriers and aligns with how other countries schedule elections
objection: Even if schools close and some employers reduce operations, many low-income workers still face the same choice between missing work and voting on limited breaks, so the holiday does not reliably remove the barrier. International practice does not change the fact that federal law in the U.S. leaves private workplace scheduling untouched.
